migrationNotes: Spine: put atoms on a scale. Give each nucleus a weight count (mass number), work backwards from that count to the neutrons, meet atoms of one element with different counts (isotopes), then average a mixed sample.

lesson.title: Same element, different mass

lead.text: A single atom is far too light for the gram to be a useful unit. One carbon atom weighs roughly 0.00000000000000000000002 g, and numbers like that are awkward to write, let alone compare. Chemists use a unit made for the job, the atomic mass unit, written u. It is defined so that a carbon atom with six protons and six neutrons weighs exactly 12 u.
On that scale a proton weighs about 1 u and a neutron weighs about 1 u. An electron weighs roughly a two-thousandth of a unit, so for most purposes we can ignore the electrons when we weigh an atom.

afterFigure.text: That makes the weight of an atom easy to estimate. Count the protons and neutrons in its nucleus and the total is its weight in u, near enough. The carbon atom in the picture has six of each, which makes twelve particles and a weight of about 12 u. The oxygen atom has eight of each, so it weighs about 16 u.

lead.text: Counting the heavy particles gives every nucleus a whole number, and that number has a name. The mass number, written A, is the number of protons plus the number of neutrons in a nucleus. It counts particles, so it is always a whole number. Chemists write it after the name of the element, as in carbon-12 or sodium-23.

Keep two counts apart. The atomic number Z counts protons only and names the element. The mass number A counts protons and neutrons together and tells you the weight. Writing N for the number of neutrons, A = Z + N.

afterFigure.text: The picture shows two small atoms. Helium has two protons and two neutrons, which gives it A = 4, so it is helium-4. Lithium has three protons and four neutrons, so A = 7 and it is lithium-7. Each atom's A is larger than its Z, because the neutrons are added on top of the protons that Z already counts.

lead.text: Apply the definition of the mass number to one carbon nucleus. The electrons are outside the nucleus and take no part.

The name of an atom now carries two pieces of information. Look up carbon and you find Z = 6, so every carbon atom has six protons. The name carbon-13 adds A = 13. Between them they describe the nucleus fully, including one thing that is not written down anywhere, the number of neutrons.

That number comes from the relation A = Z + N. The mass number counts the protons as well as the neutrons, so taking the protons off leaves the neutrons. Written as a rule, N = A − Z. The next two examples use this rule on one atom each, the first with every step shown and the second with a step left for you.

diagram.alt: Three carbon nuclei drawn as rows of particles, carbon-12, carbon-13 and carbon-14. Each has six protons, and the rest of the row are neutrons. Brackets mark the mass number A over the whole row, Z under the protons and N under the neutrons.
diagram.caption: Each dot is one particle in the nucleus. The protons are the same in every case, so the neutrons are what is left when Z is taken off A.

steps.headline: Sodium-23 has atomic number 11. How many neutrons does it have?

workedSteps.text: The mass number is the protons plus the neutrons.
Move the protons across to leave the neutrons.

steps.headline: Find the neutrons in an atom of chlorine-35, atomic number 17.

workedSteps.text: Mass number and atomic number are given.

lead.text: Go back to the chlorine atom from the last example. Chlorine-35 has 17 protons and 18 neutrons. Chlorine-37 also has 17 protons, so it is chlorine too, but its mass number is 37 and so it has 20 neutrons, two more. The two atoms share an atomic number and differ in mass number.

Atoms of one element that differ in their number of neutrons are called isotopes. Nearly every element comes as a mixture of isotopes. The extra neutrons change an isotope's weight and leave its chemistry almost untouched, because chemical behaviour is set by the electrons, and these atoms have the same number of those.

afterFigure.text: In the picture, compare the two chlorine atoms ring by ring. The ring particles match and the nucleus does not. This is the answer to the puzzle that opened the lesson. The heavier carbon atoms are carbon-13 and carbon-14, isotopes of carbon with extra neutrons.

lead.text: Isotopes are named by their mass numbers. Think about what two atoms of one element can differ in.
Use the same move as in the sodium and chlorine examples: the mass number counts the protons too.

steps.headline: The average mass of a sample

lead.text: A pinch of any element holds billions of atoms, usually of more than one isotope. Chlorine is the standard example. About three atoms in every four are chlorine-35 and the rest are chlorine-37, so no single chlorine atom weighs the 35.5 u that the periodic table lists for it.

That listed number is the average atomic mass, the average weight of an atom in a natural sample. It lies between the weights of the isotopes and sits closer to the common one. With equal numbers of two isotopes it is the number halfway between them. With more of one kind it is pulled towards that kind. This is why the numbers in the periodic table are rarely whole numbers, even though every single nucleus has a whole-number mass number.

diagram.caption: Four chlorine atoms on a mass scale. The dashed line is their average. It sits nearer the pile with more atoms. Use the buttons to change the mix.

lesson.orientation: Distinguish mass number, isotopes and the average mass of a mixture.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Some instruments can weigh atoms one at a time. A chemist feeds in a pinch of carbon, and each atom is pulled through the machine and given a weight. Nearly every atom comes out at the same value. A small share come out heavier, and a few come out heavier still.

The last lesson showed that an atom is carbon whenever it has six protons. So the heavier atoms are carbon too, and the extra weight has to come from somewhere other than the protons. The neutrons are the only particles left that could add it, since electrons weigh almost nothing.

This lesson follows that clue. We find a way to put a number on an atom's weight and use it to count the neutrons in a nucleus. Then we see why one element can have atoms of several weights, and what that means for a sample that holds billions of them.

diagram.caption: A made-up sample of 18 carbon atoms, sorted by weight. A real sample has far more atoms in the lightest pile than here.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find an atom's neutrons from its mass number, and say why one element can have atoms of different mass.
intro.whyItMatters: The weight of an atom is what lets chemists measure out a chemical by weighing it.

recap.keyIdea: The mass number counts protons plus neutrons, so the neutrons are A − Z. Isotopes share a proton count but differ in neutrons, and an element's average atomic mass is the average over its isotopes.

blocks.text: Back at the weighing machine, the heavier carbon atoms now have an explanation. You found 18 neutrons in chlorine-35 and 22 in potassium-41 by taking the atomic number off the mass number. You also saw that equal numbers of 12 u and 14 u atoms average 13 u.

recap.nextHook: Electrons weigh next to nothing in all this, yet they are the particles that move when atoms meet. The next lesson follows an atom as it gains or loses electrons and keeps a running count of its charge.

questions.prompt: A carbon nucleus has 6 protons and 7 neutrons. What is its mass number?
hints: Add the particles in the nucleus.
Use A = protons + neutrons.
Add 6 + 7.
questions.onCorrect: 13. The mass number is the proton count plus the neutron count: 6 + 7.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the neutron count alone. The mass number counts the protons as well.
That includes the six electrons, which are outside the nucleus.

questions.prompt: Chlorine-35 has atomic number 17. How many neutrons does it have?
hints: Use N = A − Z.
Mass number counts protons and neutrons together.
Subtract 17 from 35.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Subtract 17 protons from mass number 35: 18 neutrons.

questions.onCorrect: 18. Neutrons are the mass number minus the atomic number: N = A − Z.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the mass number. It counts the protons too, so the neutrons are fewer.
That adds the atomic number. Protons are part of the mass number already, so take them away.

questions.prompt: Oxygen-16 and oxygen-18 are isotopes. What differs?
hints: Compare the two names. What does the number after each name count?
Both atoms are oxygen. What does that tell you about their protons?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both have eight protons; oxygen-18 has two more neutrons.

questions.onCorrect: Isotopes share protons and differ in neutrons, so the mass number changes and the element does not.

misconceptions.feedback: Both have eight protons. That is what makes them both oxygen.
Both are oxygen, so both use the symbol O.

questions.prompt: A sample has equal numbers of atoms of approximate mass 12 u and 14 u. What is its average mass in u?
hints: Give the two masses equal weight.
Half the atoms contribute each mass.
questions.onCorrect: 13 u. With equal numbers of each, the average is the mean of the two masses.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the masses. An average divides by how many there are as well.
That is one of the two masses. With equal numbers of each, the average sits between them.

questions.prompt: An oxygen-18 ion still has 8 protons. How many neutrons does it have?
hints: The ion's charge does not change its nucleus.
Mass number counts protons and neutrons together.
Take the protons off the mass number.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Charge does not affect mass number: 18 − 8 = 10.

questions.onCorrect: 10. Charge does not change the mass number, so neutrons are still A − Z.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the mass number. It still includes the protons.
That adds the protons. They are already counted in the mass number.

questions.prompt: An element's average atomic mass is 10.8 u. What does this tell you?
hints: Separate a sample average from one atom's mass number.
